scenes.title: Built for a crossing
scenes.narration: In Belfast, during fitting out, the hull fills the frame. Titanic was nearly two hundred and seventy metres long. That length made the Atlantic crossing possible at a scale few people had experienced.

scenes.title: A hull divided
scenes.narration: Look past the paint and the rows of windows. Behind the steel were fifteen transverse bulkheads. Imagine sixteen spaces arranged along the ship, one behind the other. A local leak could be kept local.

scenes.title: Separate spaces
scenes.narration: In the machinery spaces, watertight doors could be shut between compartments. It was a practical defence against flooding. Its effectiveness depended on how many spaces filled and how high the water could rise.

scenes.title: A crossing in four stops
scenes.narration: Titanic left Southampton, called at Cherbourg, and stopped off Queenstown in Ireland. The next port was New York. The route joined a familiar traffic lane, carrying people with very different reasons for getting to America.

scenes.title: The boat deck
scenes.narration: Up on the boat deck were twenty boats, including four collapsibles. The rules in force still allowed a ship this large to sail with too few places. That gap was built into the crossing.

scenes.title: Ice ahead
scenes.narration: On Sunday, wireless messages began to describe ice in the Atlantic. Some reached the bridge. The evening message from Mesaba described ice close to Titanic's route. The British inquiry found that it never reached the bridge.

scenes.title: A calm sea
scenes.narration: It was a clear night, without moonlight. The sea was unusually calm. Breaking water at an iceberg's base might have drawn a white line. That night there was little to outline the ice.

scenes.title: Ice straight ahead
scenes.narration: The lookouts finally made out an iceberg straight ahead. A warning went to the bridge. The ship began to turn. There was enough movement for the bow to swing, but it did not clear the starboard side.

scenes.title: Under the surface
scenes.narration: For people high in the ship, the contact could seem minor. Down where the steel met the sea, the damage ran across enough of the forward hull to let water into several spaces at once.

scenes.title: Five spaces take water
scenes.narration: The inquiry concluded that the collision opened the five forward compartments to the sea. Titanic could remain afloat with the first four flooded. The fifth changed what would happen next, even if the doors did their job.

scenes.title: Water reaches the next space
scenes.narration: As the bow sank lower, water rose to the top of the forward bulkheads. Then it spilled into the spaces behind them. The ship's weight shifted towards the bow, and the process could continue from one compartment to the next.

scenes.title: A signal in the dark
scenes.narration: Harold Bride, the junior wireless operator, found his colleague Jack Phillips at work. Bride later told the American inquiry that Phillips had felt the ship tremble and stop. At first, he thought she might have to return to Belfast.

scenes.title: The call goes out
scenes.narration: Captain Smith gave the operators the ship's position. Phillips began sending distress calls. The transmitter could reach ships beyond the horizon. Anyone who answered still had to come the rest of the way by sea.

scenes.title: Carpathia turns
scenes.narration: Carpathia's wireless operator brought the call to his captain. Arthur Rostron ordered his ship to turn and steam towards Titanic at full speed. He would have to thread his own ship through the ice that Titanic had hit.

scenes.title: Two ships, two clocks
scenes.narration: On Carpathia, preparations began for passengers who might arrive injured or cold. On Titanic, crew were uncovering the boats. One ship had to close the distance. On the other, every minute was lowering the deck towards the water.

scenes.title: Down to the boats
scenes.narration: Early in the evacuation, the boat deck was still high above the water. To leave, people had to step into a boat hanging on ropes. Under their feet Titanic still seemed solid, and the open sea was a long way down.

scenes.title: Twelve in a boat built for forty
scenes.narration: Emergency boat Number One had room for forty. The inquiry found it went down with twelve people. By the time it was on the sea, those empty places were beyond the reach of the crowd on deck.

scenes.title: Getting to the boat deck
scenes.narration: A seat was useless to anyone who could not reach it. Third-class passengers survived at a lower rate. The inquiry pointed to the difficulty of getting passengers up from quarters at the far ends of the ship.

scenes.title: A letter in a jacket
scenes.narration: Seven-year-old Eva Hart went into a lifeboat wearing her father's jacket. Inside was a letter she and her mother had written that night. Eva and her mother survived. Her father did not.

scenes.title: The bow drops
scenes.narration: As the bow went down, the forward deck became harder to use. The final collapsible boats became a struggle of their own. Passengers still aboard were running out of deck and running out of ways off it.

scenes.title: The lights go out
scenes.narration: At about two twenty in the morning, Titanic was gone. More than fifteen hundred people died in the disaster. For those in the boats, the night was not over. Their next hope was a light on the horizon.

scenes.title: The first boat found
scenes.narration: The light came from a lifeboat. Just as Rostron went to pick it up, another iceberg appeared ahead. Carpathia turned again and brought the first boat alongside at about four ten by its own clock.

scenes.title: The people rescued
scenes.narration: About seven hundred people survived. Many of those pictured here still had a journey to make after coming aboard Carpathia. The first question had been how to get off Titanic. Then came the wait to be found.

scenes.title: What capacity could and could not do
scenes.narration: The boats never had enough room for everyone. Yet the total who survived fell well below even that limited capacity. The difference reflects the time, access and decisions that determined which places could actually be used.

scenes.title: The news reaches shore
scenes.displayNote: 16 April 1912 · New York Times front page
scenes.narration: On shore, early reports gave numbers that were still changing. Investigators in Britain and the United States then heard from people who had been there. They asked what had gone wrong, from the ice messages to the boats.

scenes.title: The rules change
scenes.narration: In nineteen fourteen, an international safety convention was adopted. It addressed lifesaving equipment, radio and other safeguards. The disaster also led to an international ice patrol. A future ship should have earlier warnings and a better chance to get everyone off.

scenes.title: Seventy-three years later
scenes.narration: For more than seven decades, the wreck itself was missing. In nineteen eighty-five, a Franco-American expedition searched the seabed. On a video monitor, amid the debris, the team saw an object that looked like one of Titanic's boilers.

scenes.title: The first clue
scenes.narration: The boiler helped confirm that the searchers were looking at Titanic's debris. The wreck was far below the surface, and the bow and stern lay apart. The ship they found was no longer the intact outline known from departure photographs.

scenes.title: The bow on the seabed
scenes.narration: The following year, another expedition returned with a submersible. Its cameras picked out recognisable parts of the ship in darkness. The wreck preserved things no witness could see in the final minutes. The photographs and testimony preserve others.

scenes.title: The distance between a deck and a boat
scenes.narration: The story began with too few places on the water. It ended with rescuers lifting people from separate boats, hours after the ship had gone. Titanic had made an ocean crossing feel ordinary. That night, even the distance from deck to boat could be too far.
